questions.q: A simple DC electric motor is best described as a device that transforms which form of energy into which other form?
options: Rotational kinetic energy into electrical potential energy
Electrical potential energy into rotational kinetic energy
Chemical potential energy into magnetic field energy
Mechanical kinetic energy directly into heat energy
questions.explanation: An electric motor is a device that transforms electrical potential energy into rotational kinetic energy by passing a current through a coil in a magnetic field. Running the same machine backwards — rotation in, electrical energy out — gives a generator.

questions.q: In a simple DC motor the coil is wound onto a frame called the armature. What name is given to the armature and coil together, and what name is given to the stationary magnets fixed to the casing?
options: Armature and coil are the stator; the stationary magnets are the rotor
Armature and coil are the rotor; the stationary magnets are the stator
Both the coil and the magnets are called the rotor
Both the coil and the magnets are called the commutator
questions.explanation: The coil is wound onto a frame (the armature) and the armature and coil together are known as the rotor — the rotating part. The magnets are fixed to the casing and are stationary, so they are the stator. Students often wrongly call the magnets the rotor; the magnets do not move.

questions.q: The split-ring commutator and the brushes of a DC motor together form a mechanical switch. What does this mechanical switch do?
options: It changes the direction of the current through the coil every half turn so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction
It increases the magnitude of the current through the coil to boost the torque
It keeps the current in the coil flowing in one constant direction throughout the whole rotation
It converts the alternating supply into a steady direct current for the coil
questions.explanation: The split-ring commutator and the brushes form a mechanical switch that changes the direction of the current through the coil every half turn, so that the coil continues rotating in the same direction. Without this reversal the coil would only rock back and forth.

questions.q: From memory, using the textbook's description: what would happen to the coil if the current through the coil did NOT change its direction of flow, and why does the coil keep rotating through the position where the torque is almost zero?
keyPoints: If the current through the coil did not change direction, the coil would rock back and forth about the position where the torque is almost zero.
The momentum of the coil keeps it rotating even though the torque is very small (near zero) in that position.
Just after that position the commutator changes the direction of the current, the forces reverse, and the torque stays clockwise — so the coil keeps rotating the same way.
questions.explanation: If you recalled 'rock back and forth without reversal', 'momentum carries it through the near-zero-torque position', and 'the commutator reverses the current so the torque stays in the same direction', grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: Why are the brushes of a DC motor made of graphite, and what practical problem do the brushes solve?
options: Graphite is strongly magnetic, and the brushes store charge to drive the coil
Graphite is a form of carbon that conducts electricity and is also used as a lubricant; the brushes stop the connecting wires from becoming tangled
Graphite is an electrical insulator, and the brushes permanently break the circuit
Graphite is ferromagnetic, and the brushes strengthen the external magnetic field
questions.explanation: Graphite, used in the brushes, is a form of carbon that conducts electricity and is also used as a lubricant, so it slides smoothly against the rotating commutator. The brushes connect the commutator to the DC source of emf and are necessary to stop the connecting wires from becoming tangled.

questions.q: A coil contains 15 loops and its plane is sitting at an angle of 30° to the direction of a magnetic field of 7.6 mT. The coil has dimensions 8.0 cm by 12.0 cm and a current of 15 mA passes through it. Determine the magnitude of the torque acting on the coil.
questions.given: \(n = 15\) loops,  \(B = 7.6\,\mathrm{mT} = 7.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{T}\),  \(I = 15\,\mathrm{mA} = 1.5\times10^{-2}\,\mathrm{A}\),  \(A = 0.080 \times 0.120 = 9.6\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}\),  \(\theta = 30^\circ\) (angle between coil plane and field)
questions.explanation: Direct substitution into \(\tau = nBIA\cos\theta\), with \(\theta\) measured from the plane of the coil to the field (so cosine, not sine). The unit is newton metres because torque is a force times a distance. Applying the right-hand push rule to the left-hand side gives anticlockwise rotation.

questions.q: A rectangular coil of 20 turns and area 5×10⁻³ m² carries a current of 2 A in a magnetic field of 0.1 T. Calculate the maximum torque on the coil, and state the orientation of the coil at which this maximum occurs.
questions.given: \(n = 20\),  \(A = 5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m^2}\),  \(I = 2\,\mathrm{A}\),  \(B = 0.1\,\mathrm{T}\); maximum when \(\cos\theta = 1\) (coil plane parallel to field)
working: Maximum torque occurs when \(\cos\theta = 1\), i.e. the plane of the coil is parallel to the field, so \(\tau_{\max} = nBIA\)
questions.explanation: Maximum torque is at \(\cos\theta = 1\) — when the coil plane lies parallel to the field — so \(\tau_{\max} = nBIA = 0.02\,\mathrm{N\,m}\). The trap is thinking the maximum is when the plane is perpendicular to the field; that is the zero-torque position.

questions.q: Beyond increasing the current or field strength, how does winding two or more coils onto the armature affect a DC motor, and what does a stator with curved magnetic poles achieve?
options: Multiple coils increase the average torque and make the motor run more smoothly, while curved poles keep the force at right angles to the line of action for longer, keeping the torque at its maximum value for longer
Multiple coils reduce the average torque, while curved poles weaken the magnetic field of the stator
Multiple coils reverse the current automatically, removing the need for a commutator, while curved poles act as the brushes
Multiple coils convert the DC motor into an AC motor, while curved poles generate the back emf
questions.explanation: Two or more coils wound on the armature increase the average torque and make the motor run more smoothly than a single-coil motor (each coil needs its own pair of commutator segments). A stator with curved magnetic poles keeps the force at right angles to the line joining the point of application and the axle for longer, keeping the torque at its maximum for longer.

questions.q: Why does a simple DC motor require a split-ring commutator, whereas a simple AC motor uses slip rings?
options: Because the DC supply current flows in only one direction, so the reversal in the coil must be forced mechanically by the split ring; an AC supply already reverses direction on its own, so the slip rings need only maintain a continuous connection
Because slip rings are cheaper and DC motors must use the more expensive split ring
Because an AC motor has no magnetic field and needs slip rings to create one
Because a commutator reverses current, and an AC motor also needs to reverse its coil current every half turn
questions.explanation: A DC supply flows in only one direction, so the coil current can only be reversed at the dead point by mechanically swapping the connections — the split-ring commutator does this. An AC supply already alternates (50 times a second in Australia), so an AC motor needs only slip rings — continuous, unsplit rings that maintain the connection without reversing anything. Never say an AC motor 'has a commutator'.

questions.q: From memory, explain the role of the split-ring commutator in a simple DC motor as a full marks chain — include WHEN it reverses the current and WHY that matters.
keyPoints: As the coil rotates toward the zero-torque position (its plane perpendicular to the field), the torque falls to zero and the coil's momentum carries it past this dead point.
Without reversal the unchanged forces would push the coil back, so it would oscillate about the zero-torque position instead of rotating.

The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn, exactly at the zero-torque position, so the force on each side reverses and the torque keeps acting in the same rotational direction — turning oscillation into continuous, one-directional rotation.
questions.explanation: Full marks needs four links: set up the torque from the motor effect, identify the zero-torque (dead) point as the problem, describe the commutator mechanism physically, and tie the reversal to the result (continuous rotation). Never let 'reverses the current' stand alone — always attach the when (every half-turn, at the zero-torque position) and the why.
